# The Replica Skill

Eleven Claude skills that clone any app. They're free, MIT-licensed, and require no signup, API key, or connection of any kind.

# Autoresearch

Turn Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into a relentless improvement engine.

This is based on Karpathy's autoresearch idea: give the agent a constraint, a mechanical metric, and let it iterate autonomously. The gains compound.

You set the goal. The agent runs the loop. You wake up to results.

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that never quits.

Autoresearch supports Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse for the core skill, bundled runtime, installation, and verification surface. Hook guardrails ship for two of them: Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

**Fork-and-flush.** Metric loops escape plateaus the way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) do. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness). The other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided mode: R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it answers with FORK before it gives up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

Bumblebee

Bumblebee is a read-only inventory collector that gathers package, extension, and developer-tool metadata from macOS and Linux developer endpoints.

It answers a narrow question that comes up during supply-chain response: when an advisory names a package, extension, or version, which developer machines currently show a match in their on-disk metadata?

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. But supply-chain response often needs a different view—messy local state spread across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee turns that scattered on-disk state into structured NDJSON component records. Given an exposure catalog, it flags exact matches, enabling fast, read-only exposure checks when responders already know what they're looking for.

SkillsBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across a range of domains. The idea is to measure how much a model's ability to solve complex, real-world tasks improves when it has specialized Skills available.

To make the evaluation more realistic, we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting that mirrors production environments, where many Skills are installed at once. In the original setup, each task comes with only the one specialized Skill tied to it. In our modified version, every task runs in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, with every other experimental condition held constant. The point of this setting is to see whether an agent can find, select, and orchestrate the right Skills from a large installed pool on its own, and assemble them into an effective workflow for a complex task.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Compared with the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points while cutting token consumption by 29.6% and tool calls by 33.1%.

## Releases

It works in any Git repo with no setup.
